answer: The BLIS configuration space has strong structure that enables efficient search. The 6-knob space (1800 configs) reduces to an effective space of ~120 configs because: (1) block_size=32 always dominates 16 — larger blocks waste less memory per allocation, giving 27% better rps and 54% better ttft_p99 at kv=3000; (2) scheduler is a minor knob — sjf gives ~5% better throughput but ~13% worse tail latency vs fcfs, creating a genuine but small Pareto trade-off only under single-instance contention; (3) max_num_running_reqs has a threshold at 128 above which performance is identical; below it (32, 64) causes queuing that hurts all metrics. The dominant axis is the TP-vs-instances trade-off: at 8 GPUs, tp=8×1 achieves 30.24 rps but 1122ms ttft_p99, while tp=4×2 achieves 26.78 rps with just 29.57ms ttft_p99 — a 2.7× throughput-for-latency trade-off. Higher TP always gives better throughput per GPU but concentrates load onto fewer instances, causing tail latency to spike. KV blocks show a per-config threshold effect: below threshold, preemptions degrade both rps and ttft; above it, extra blocks are wasted. The Pareto front has ~30-35 configs spanning GPU counts 1-8, KV blocks 2000-4000, and both schedulers. A 200-evaluation search (11% of the space) finds this front by: (a) surveying all 15 tp/inst combos at ceiling, (b) sweeping kv×maxr for each combo, (c) testing sjf for single-instance configs where it creates trade-offs.
